entries.label: Physical Akida studies report real latency, power, and energy measurements, but they reuse BrainChip's existing QuantizeML and CNN2SNN toolchain rather than introducing a new low-timestep rate-coded ANN-to-SNN conversion algorithm. entries.boundary: Named physical AKD1000 or Akida PCIe hardware. Individual studies use different boundaries. Ziegler et al. report measured Akida inference and forward-pass latency plus Akida power. Lunghi et al. report device energy per frame and explicitly expose idle-floor power. Putra and Shafique report application-level latency, power, and energy on AKD1000.

entries.boundary: Architecture semantics, not an impossibility theorem. Other event-driven chips, including Speck2e, may be timestep-free, which is a different execution model rather than proof of discrete mixed layer horizons.

entries.label: The overwhelming majority of published event-vision pipelines accumulate the event-camera stream into a dense frame or voxel-grid buffer over a fixed time window before any neural network sees it.
An event camera's raw AER output can be consumed directly by an event-driven spiking chip with no frame buffer in between, e.g. Speck's on-die DVS array feeding its co-integrated DYNAP-CNN core.

The only conversion-based event-vision deployment reaching physical silicon (Massa et al. 2020, Loihi DVS Gesture) first pre-accumulates DVS events into frames off-chip, trains a conventional DNN on those frames, and only then applies classical rate-coded ANN-to-SNN conversion (SNN Toolbox) before Loihi execution. No paper pairs a genuinely native (non-frame-reconstructed) event stream with rate-coded conversion on physical hardware.

Native DVS event streams (DVS128 Gesture/Gait, N-MNIST) are trained directly via BPTT (Sinabs+sinabs-exodus, SpikingJelly) and deployed to physical Speck/DYNAP-CNN and CRI FPGA hardware with measured on-chip accuracy and energy; the Speck1 paper's own head-to-head comparison found direct BPTT training gives higher on-chip accuracy than ANN2SNN conversion on the same chip.
